question: How do I hire a fractional CRO for a proptech business?
body:
## Direct Answer
Hiring a fractional CRO for a proptech business means engaging a part-time revenue leader who owns your sales, marketing, and customer success motion for a fraction of a full-time executive's cost, typically two to four days a week under a monthly retainer. Prioritize candidates with proven experience selling into real estate, construction, or property-management buyers, because those cycles, stakeholders, and procurement rhythms differ sharply from generic B2B SaaS. Define the revenue problem first, scope the engagement to 90-day outcomes, and vet for pattern-matched proptech GTM experience over generic executive polish.

Proptech companies sit at an awkward crossroads: they sell modern software into an industry that still runs on relationships, long escrow-style sales cycles, and fragmented buyer committees spanning brokers, property owners, facilities teams, and IT. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives an early or mid-stage proptech venture senior GTM leadership without the roughly $250K–$400K fully loaded cost of a full-time hire. The trick is matching the right operator to your specific revenue stage, then structuring the engagement so their part-time hours produce full-time accountability. This guide walks through when to hire, how to source and vet, what to pay, and how to structure the first 90 days — and, just as important, the failure modes that quietly drain months of runway when a founder skips the disciplined version of this process.

Before you post a role or ping a marketplace, it helps to internalize why proptech is its own animal. The category spans wildly different sub-worlds: multifamily operations software, commercial leasing platforms, construction-tech and jobsite tools, mortgage and title automation, short-term-rental management, ESG and building-performance analytics, and iBuying-adjacent transaction tools. Each has a distinct buyer, a distinct budget owner, and a distinct integration surface. A fractional CRO who thrived in one of these may be only marginally more useful than a generalist in another. So the real question is not "how do I hire a fractional CRO" in the abstract — it is "how do I hire the fractional CRO whose scar tissue matches my exact slice of proptech." Everything below is built around answering that sharper question.

## When does a proptech company actually need a fractional CRO instead of a VP of Sales?
The distinction matters because hiring the wrong seniority wastes both money and momentum. A VP of Sales executes a known playbook — they hire reps, run the pipeline, and hit a number against a motion that already works. A CRO builds the motion itself: aligning marketing, sales, and customer success into one revenue engine, deciding which segments to chase, and setting pricing and packaging. Early proptech companies usually do not yet know their repeatable motion, which is exactly the CRO-shaped problem. If you already have product-market fit and a working pipeline and simply need more capacity, a VP or a strong sales manager is the cheaper, better answer.

The fractional version fits a narrow but common band: you have found early traction (often founder-led sales past $500K–$2M ARR), you need to systematize and scale it, but you cannot yet justify or afford a $350K executive plus equity. In proptech specifically, the fractional CRO earns their keep by untangling the multi-stakeholder sale — figuring out whether you sell to the property owner, the operator, the broker, or the tenant, and building the segmentation and messaging that reflects that. That strategic disambiguation is worth far more than incremental rep capacity. For a deeper look at the stage question, see our guide to [when to hire your first revenue leader](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10241).

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a proptech business — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9257-b1.jpg)


A useful gut check: if your revenue problem is "we don't know why deals stall or which segment to double down on," that is a strategy problem a fractional CRO solves. If it is "we know exactly what works and just need more people doing it," you have an execution problem, and a fractional CRO is over-engineered for it.

There is also a middle case worth naming, because many proptech founders sit squarely in it: you have a repeatable-ish motion for one segment but you are trying to cross into a second, structurally different buyer. A common example is a company that nailed selling to independent property managers and now wants to land regional owner-operators or a national REIT. The first motion — transactional, self-serve-adjacent, champion-led — does not transfer to the second, which is committee-driven, procurement-gated, and security-reviewed. That transition is a classic fractional-CRO assignment: you do not need a permanent enterprise sales org yet, but you do need someone who has run enterprise real-estate deals to architect the pilot-to-rollout motion, build the mutual action plan template, and train the founder to sell higher. Recognizing that you have two motions rather than one is often the single most valuable diagnosis a fractional CRO delivers, and it is precisely the kind of insight a VP of Sales, hired to run a single known playbook, is not positioned to surface.

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a proptech business — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9257-b2.jpg)


Finally, weigh the honest downside of going fractional too early. A part-time leader cannot manufacture demand that the product and market do not yet support. If you have not validated that anyone will pay real money to solve the problem, no CRO — fractional or full-time — fixes that, and the retainer becomes an expensive way to postpone the harder product conversation. Fractional CRO leadership amplifies a signal; it does not create one from noise.

## What proptech-specific experience should you screen for?
The single biggest hiring mistake is treating "CRO" as a generic credential. A brilliant fractional CRO who scaled a horizontal SaaS tool may flounder in proptech because the buying committee, sales cycle, and integration expectations are alien to them. Real estate buyers evaluate software against decades of entrenched processes and thin technology budgets. Deals routinely involve a champion at the operator level, a skeptical CFO or asset manager controlling the budget, and an IT or facilities gatekeeper worried about integration with legacy systems like Yardi, MRI, or RealPage.

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a proptech business — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9257-b3.jpg)


Screen hard for three things. First, direct GTM experience selling into your slice of the market — multifamily, commercial, construction tech, mortgage and title, or facilities management are meaningfully different worlds. Second, comfort with long, committee-driven sales cycles measured in quarters, not weeks, and the patience-plus-forecasting discipline that requires. Third, a network. A large part of a proptech CRO's value is warm introductions to owner-operators, REITs, brokerages, and channel partners; ask for specific relationships they can activate in your first quarter, not vague claims of "deep industry connections."

Be equally alert to red flags: a candidate who describes proptech as "just SaaS with a real estate logo," who has never navigated a procurement process gated by a property-management platform, or who talks exclusively about top-of-funnel volume while ignoring the deal-desk and implementation friction that kills proptech renewals. The best fractional proptech CROs speak fluently about both the software motion and the physical-world realities — tenant turnover, lease cycles, capital-expenditure approval calendars — that shape when and why buyers actually sign. Our breakdown of [multi-stakeholder B2B sales](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10877) covers the committee dynamics in more detail.

It is worth being concrete about what "proptech fluency" sounds like in an interview, because polished generalists can fake a lot. Ask a candidate to walk you through the last real estate deal they closed end to end: who the economic buyer was, how the budget was approved, which internal system the software had to integrate with, how long security and procurement review took, and what nearly killed the deal. A pattern-matched operator answers in specifics — "the asset manager wanted a Yardi write-back, legal snagged on the data-processing terms, and we lost six weeks to their annual budget freeze." A generalist gives you funnel abstractions. Also probe for understanding of proptech's seasonality and capital cycles: leasing seasons, fiscal-year budget windows, and the way a single macro shift in interest rates or occupancy can freeze an entire segment's buying for two quarters. A CRO who has lived through a real-estate downturn brings forecasting realism that a pure-boom-era SaaS operator often lacks.

Screen just as carefully on the post-sale side, because proptech churn hides in implementation. Many proptech products require data migration from incumbent systems, on-site training of non-technical staff, and integration with hardware — access control, smart-building sensors, sub-metering. A revenue leader who owns only new bookings and ignores onboarding will leave you with a leaky bucket where signed logos never fully deploy and never renew. Ask how the candidate has previously aligned customer success and implementation with sales so that "closed-won" actually converts to "live and expanding." In proptech, the CRO's ownership of net revenue retention is frequently where the real economics live, not in logo acquisition. A candidate who cannot speak to onboarding friction, reference-account development, and expansion within a property portfolio is telling you they have only ever managed the front half of the revenue engine.

## How do you source and vet fractional CRO candidates?
Sourcing runs through three main channels, each with tradeoffs. Fractional executive networks and marketplaces (such as Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Bolster, and Continuum) offer vetted, ready-to-engage operators and handle contracting, but their rosters skew generalist, so you must filter aggressively for proptech depth. Warm referrals from proptech investors, accelerators, and founder communities tend to produce the highest-fit candidates because the referrer already understands the domain. Direct outreach to former revenue leaders at proptech companies you admire is the slowest path but can surface exactly the pattern-matched operator you want.

Whatever the channel, run a structured vetting process rather than a vibes-based chat. The diagram below shows a clean path from problem definition to a scoped engagement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Define the revenue problem] --> B[Write a 90 day outcome brief]
  B --> C[Source three to five candidates]
  C --> D[Screen for proptech GTM experience]
  D --> E[Reference check two past clients]
  E --> F[Run a paid diagnostic sprint]
  F --> G[Scope retainer and success metrics]
  G --> H[Sign and onboard]
```

References are non-negotiable and should be past clients, not colleagues. Ask each reference two pointed questions: what measurable revenue change happened during the engagement, and what did the CRO fail to deliver or get wrong. A reference who cannot name a single shortcoming is either not candid or did not work closely with the person. Pay special attention to whether the fractional CRO left behind durable systems — a documented sales process, a working forecast, hired-and-ramped reps — versus a dependency that collapses the moment they leave.

A paid diagnostic sprint is the best de-risking tool available. Before committing to a six- or twelve-month retainer, engage the candidate for a two-to-four-week paid audit of your revenue engine. You get a concrete deliverable — a GTM assessment, pipeline diagnosis, and prioritized plan — and a live look at how they think, communicate, and prioritize. If the diagnostic is sharp and specific to proptech, extend the engagement. If it is a recycled generic template, you have learned that cheaply. See our [revenue diagnostic framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11455) for what a strong audit should surface.

Two practical additions make the vetting process meaningfully stronger. First, insist on a working-session interview rather than a presentation. Put a real, messy slice of your pipeline in front of the candidate and watch them reason live: which deals they would triage, which segment they would kill, what they would ask your reps. This reveals judgment that a polished deck cannot. A strong operator will start asking sharp, uncomfortable questions about your unit economics and win rates within minutes; a weak one will retreat to frameworks. Second, check for conflicts and concentration risk before you fall in love with a candidate. Because fractional CROs run several clients at once, confirm in writing that none of their current or recent clients compete with you, and gauge how many concurrent engagements they carry — beyond three or four, their attention thins and your "committed days" become theoretical. Ask specifically how they protect focus for each client and how they handle a quarter-end crunch when two clients need them simultaneously.

Do not skip a lightweight background and reputation check, either. The fractional executive market has grown fast, and the title "CRO" is self-conferred as often as it is earned. Verify the scale of the outcomes a candidate claims — an operator who says they "drove revenue from two to twenty million" should be able to explain their exact role, the team around them, and what portion of that growth their decisions actually caused. Cross-reference their claims against the references and, where possible, against a mutual connection in the proptech community. The goal is not to distrust everyone; it is to make sure the person who impressed you in a one-hour conversation has genuinely done the thing you are about to pay them to do again.

## What should a fractional proptech CRO engagement cost, and how is it structured?
Fractional CRO compensation typically runs on a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days. Market ranges vary widely by experience and market, but retainers commonly land between $8,000 and $20,000 per month for a two-to-three-day-per-week commitment, with senior operators in hot markets commanding more. Many engagements add a performance component — equity, or a bonus tied to pipeline, bookings, or net revenue retention — to align incentives without the full cash burden of a salaried executive. Always confirm current market rates directly with candidates and marketplaces rather than anchoring on a fixed figure, since compensation moves with demand and specialization.

Structure the engagement around outcomes, not hours logged. A well-scoped agreement names the specific revenue problems being solved, the deliverables expected in the first 90 days, the cadence of check-ins, and clear success metrics — pipeline created, sales-cycle compression, win-rate improvement, or a defined and documented GTM motion. Time-and-materials billing invites drift; outcome-based scoping keeps everyone honest. The table below compares the common models.

| Model | Typical use | Watch-out |
|-------|-------------|-----------|
| Monthly retainer | Ongoing GTM leadership | Scope creep if outcomes are vague |
| Diagnostic sprint | Two to four week audit | Not a substitute for execution |
| Retainer plus equity | Cash-tight early stage | Dilution and alignment terms |
| Milestone-based | Specific project or launch | Requires crisp milestone definitions |

Contract length deserves thought. Month-to-month gives you flexibility but weakens the CRO's ability to make long-horizon bets. A three-to-six-month initial term with a clear renewal checkpoint tends to balance commitment and optionality. Build in a defined offboarding path so that whenever the engagement ends, the knowledge, systems, and relationships transfer to your team rather than walking out the door.

Think carefully about the performance component, because proptech's long cycles distort naive incentive design. If your sales cycle runs six to nine months, a bonus tied to closed bookings in the first quarter will pay out on deals the CRO inherited, not deals they built — and will pay nothing on the pipeline they legitimately created that closes after they are gone. Tie early incentives to leading indicators the CRO genuinely controls (qualified pipeline created, sales-cycle stage progression, forecast accuracy, documented process milestones) and reserve bookings- or retention-based upside for longer engagements where the timeline actually lets their work mature. When equity is on the table, keep the grant modest and proportional to a part-time role, vest it over the engagement's real duration rather than granting it upfront, and be explicit about what happens to unvested equity if either side ends the engagement early.

Also budget for the true total cost, which is more than the retainer. A fractional CRO who is doing their job will want to invest in the revenue engine around them — a CRM cleanup, a sales-enablement tool, a data-enrichment source, possibly a first sales hire or an SDR. Those are the point of the exercise, not overruns, but founders sometimes anchor only on the monthly fee and get surprised. Discuss up front what discretionary spend the CRO can recommend and who approves it. The cheapest version of this hire — a low retainer with no supporting budget — often underperforms precisely because you have bought the strategist without funding the strategy.

## What does the first 90 days look like?
The opening quarter determines whether the engagement compounds or stalls. A strong fractional CRO front-loads listening and diagnosis, then moves decisively into a small number of high-leverage changes. Sprawling change agendas fail because a part-time leader cannot personally drive ten initiatives; the discipline is picking two or three that unlock the most revenue and sequencing the rest.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Days 1 to 30 diagnose] --> B[Days 31 to 60 build]
  B --> C[Days 61 to 90 prove]
  A --> D[Interview reps and buyers]
  B --> E[Fix pricing and process]
  C --> F[Show pipeline lift]
```

In the first 30 days the CRO diagnoses: interviewing reps, sitting in on live deals, talking to won and lost customers, and pressure-testing the pipeline and forecast. In proptech this includes mapping the real buying committee and identifying where deals actually stall — often at the procurement or integration gate rather than the sales conversation. Days 31 to 60 shift to building: tightening segmentation and messaging, fixing pricing and packaging, installing a real sales process and forecasting rhythm, and beginning to coach or restructure the team. Days 61 to 90 are about proving momentum — demonstrable pipeline lift, a cleaner forecast, faster cycle times, or improved win rates on the segments you chose to prioritize.

The measure of a good first quarter is not heroics but installed systems. A fractional CRO who personally closes a few big deals but leaves no repeatable motion behind has created a dependency, not an engine. The goal is that your team can run the motion when the CRO's hours eventually taper. Our guide to [building a repeatable sales motion](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11820) details what "installed" should mean in practice.

Set expectations honestly about what 90 days can and cannot deliver in a long-cycle category. If your average deal takes two quarters to close, the first 90 days will rarely show a dramatic revenue jump, and a candidate who promises one is either sandbagging you or planning to inflate the pipeline with unqualified deals. The right proof points early are structural: a clearly defined ideal customer profile, a qualification framework your reps actually use, a forecast you can trust within a reasonable band, a fixed pricing and packaging story, and a visible increase in well-qualified pipeline entering the top of the funnel. Revenue is a lagging indicator of those changes, and in proptech the lag is real. Judge the first quarter on whether the machine is measurably better built, not only on whether the number moved.

The founder's role in the first 90 days is decisive and easy to underrate. A fractional CRO with two days a week cannot succeed if they cannot get access — to your calendar, to live deals, to your reps, and to the customer conversations where the truth lives. Clear the path: introduce them internally with real authority, hand over decision rights on the areas they own, and resist the urge to overrule their process changes the moment a rep grumbles. Establish a weekly operating rhythm from day one — a standing check-in, a shared dashboard, and a short written update — so that part-time hours stay tightly coupled to full-time accountability. The engagements that fail rarely fail because the operator was weak; they fail because the founder hired a revenue leader and then quietly withheld the authority and access that leadership requires. Treat the first quarter as a two-way trial, and by day 90 you will know whether to renew, restructure, or begin the search for the full-time successor this person can help you hire.

## Related questions
### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A consultant advises and hands you a report; a fractional CRO owns the revenue number and executes as an embedded member of your leadership team, hiring, coaching, and running the motion rather than just recommending changes.

### Can one fractional CRO cover sales, marketing, and customer success?
Yes — that is the point of the CRO title. They align all three revenue functions under one strategy, though in practice they set direction and rely on your team or specialists to execute the day-to-day within each function.

### Should an early-stage proptech startup hire fractional or wait for full-time?
Fractional makes sense when you need senior GTM strategy but cannot yet justify a $300K-plus executive. Once revenue and headcount grow enough to keep a full-time CRO fully utilized, transition to a permanent hire.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to eighteen months — long enough to install a durable motion, short enough to hand off to a full-time leader once the company outgrows part-time leadership.

### What KPIs prove a fractional CRO is working?
Pipeline created, win-rate improvement, sales-cycle compression, net revenue retention, and — most importantly — a documented, repeatable motion your team can run without them.

## FAQ
**How quickly can a fractional CRO start delivering value?**
A capable operator produces a credible diagnosis and prioritized plan within the first two to four weeks, which is why a paid diagnostic sprint is such a good trial. Measurable revenue impact typically shows in the 60-to-90-day window as new process and messaging take hold.

**Do fractional CROs work with multiple clients at once?**
Yes, most carry two to four concurrent clients, which is what makes the model affordable. Confirm they have genuine bandwidth for your committed days and that none of their other clients are direct competitors.

**Should I offer equity to a fractional CRO?**
Often, especially if cash is tight. Equity aligns the CRO to long-term outcomes, but keep the grant proportional to a part-time engagement and vest it against tenure or milestones rather than granting it all upfront.

**What if the fractional CRO and my founder clash on strategy?**
Healthy tension is expected; the CRO is hired partly to challenge assumptions. Set a clear decision-rights framework upfront — who owns which calls — and hold a mid-engagement checkpoint. If the clash is fundamental and persistent, the month-to-month or short-term structure lets you part cleanly.

**How do I transition from a fractional to a full-time CRO?**
Plan it deliberately. Have the fractional CRO help scope the full-time role, interview candidates, and document the motion so the incoming leader inherits systems rather than chaos. Some fractional CROs will run the search as part of their mandate.

**Is proptech experience truly required, or is strong SaaS GTM enough?**
Strong SaaS fundamentals transfer, but proptech's committee-driven, integration-gated, capital-expenditure-timed sales cycle punishes operators who underestimate it. Prefer a candidate with direct real estate or construction-tech GTM experience; if you accept a pure-SaaS background, budget extra ramp time for them to learn the domain.

**How do I avoid getting stuck with a generalist from a marketplace?**
Filter the marketplace roster explicitly for proptech deals closed, ask for named industry relationships they can activate, and run a paid diagnostic before committing. The sprint reveals within weeks whether their expertise is real or generic.

**How many days a week should I contract for?**
Two to three days is the common sweet spot for early-stage GTM leadership — enough for the CRO to run a real operating rhythm and stay close to live deals, without paying full-time rates. One day a week rarely produces momentum in a complex proptech sale; four or more usually signals you actually need a full-time hire.

**What happens to my pipeline and relationships when the engagement ends?**
Everything the CRO built should transfer to you: documented process, forecast, playbooks, and warm relationships introduced under your brand rather than theirs. Write knowledge transfer and a defined offboarding into the contract so an ending engagement leaves an engine behind, not a vacuum.
